rationale: A wins because it keeps the story close to the facts and makes the proof burden painful in the right places. Its strongest line, "The auto-renewal has an adversary now: Ramp's agent drafts the cancellation email," gives a reporter conflict without making up a war. B has useful bones, but "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" turns one spend-volume fact into a moat thesis the update does not actually prove.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp gives away software-spend auditing for free, and plans to charge enterprises later" overstates the pricing fact. The update says an enterprise tier is coming, not that Ramp will charge for it.

"The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling." is a little too declarative. The update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not that cancellations beat renegotiations in realized dollars.
"first public dataset behind it" is plausible but not supplied. Do not call something first unless the company gave you the receipts.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" is the big overreach. The update says Ramp processes $80B and the agent scans spend; it does not prove a payments-network intelligence engine.

"payment-level visibility into $80B in annualized volume gives it transaction-native intelligence" invents the mechanism and competitive advantage. B even admits this is "not inferrable from the press release alone," then builds a headline on it anyway.
"SaaS vendors profit structurally from auto-renewals and shelfware" is likely true industry context, but it is not in the update and needs outside sourcing before it becomes a pitch spine.
The next step is too generic: "four viable shapes exist" is less useful than A telling the founder which missing data will kill the first pitch.
